questions.stem: Sparta lay in the valley of which river, between the Taygetus and Parnon ranges?
options: Alpheus
Cephissus
Achelous
Eurotas
questions.explanation: Sparta stood on the Eurotas in Laconia, with Mount Taygetus to the west and Parnon to the east. The Alpheus flows past Olympia, and the Cephissus runs through Attica and Boeotia.

questions.stem: How did the geography of Laconia help shape Spartan society?
options: Mountain barriers gave security, and the fertile valley supported a farming elite
Its long coastline and harbours made Sparta the leading naval power of Greece
Its silver mines paid for a professional army of foreign mercenaries
Poor soil forced the Spartans to found many overseas colonies to feed their people
questions.explanation: The Eurotas valley was fertile and ringed by mountains, so Sparta could rely on land worked by helots and needed no city walls for centuries. Sparta was a land power, had no great silver mines, and founded few colonies (Taras was the main one).

questions.stem: West of Mount Taygetus lay Messenia. Why was control of Messenia so important to Sparta?
options: It held the only harbour from which Spartan ships could reach the Aegean Sea
It contained Delphi, so whichever city held it controlled the oracle of Apollo there
Its marble quarries supplied the stone for Sparta's great city walls
Its rich plain gave land and helot labour that freed Spartiates to train for war
questions.explanation: Conquered Messenia gave the Spartiates fertile land worked by helots, which supported the full-time citizen soldier. Delphi is in Phocis, and Sparta had no stone walls until long after the classical period.

questions.stem: Most written evidence about Sparta comes from non-Spartans such as Herodotus, Thucydides, Xenophon, Aristotle and Plutarch. What problem does this create?
options: Outsiders often idealised or criticised Sparta to make points about their own cities
These writers could not read Doric Greek, so they misunderstood Spartan laws
All of them wrote before the Persian Wars, so they knew little about later Sparta
They relied only on Spartan official archives, which recorded nothing negative at all
questions.explanation: Spartans wrote little about themselves, so we see them through others, who used Sparta as a model or a warning. This is the 'Spartan mirage'. The writers span the fifth century BCE to about 100 CE, and Sparta kept no public archive of the kind described.

questions.stem: The phrase 'the Spartan mirage', made famous by the French scholar Francois Ollier, refers to:
options: a myth that Sparta had never been conquered before the Romans came
the Spartan claim that both of their royal houses descended from the god Apollo
the distorted, idealised image of Sparta built up by ancient writers
the heat haze that hid Spartan armies from their enemies in summer
questions.explanation: Ollier's Le mirage spartiate (1933) argued that much of what ancient writers said about Sparta was an idealised construction. Historians therefore test literary claims against archaeology and the few Spartan voices, such as Alcman and Tyrtaeus.

questions.stem: Xenophon's Constitution of the Lacedaemonians praises Spartan customs. Which point best explains why a historian should use it with care?
options: Xenophon never visited the Peloponnese and wrote only from Athenian rumours
The work was written in the Roman period, long after the customs it describes
Xenophon was a Theban who wished to justify the victory at Leuctra
Xenophon admired Sparta and was close to King Agesilaus
questions.explanation: Xenophon was an Athenian exile who served with Agesilaus and lived on an estate the Spartans gave him, so he knew Sparta well but was sympathetic. He wrote in the fourth century BCE, not the Roman period.

questions.stem: Plutarch's Life of Lycurgus, written about 100 CE, is a major source for the agoge. Which limitation matters most when using it for the sixth and fifth centuries BCE?
options: Plutarch wrote only about the kings and says nothing at all on the training of boys
Plutarch used no earlier writers and relied entirely on his own visit
Roman-era Sparta revived and exaggerated old customs, colouring his picture
Plutarch was a Spartan citizen who was forbidden to reveal the city's secrets
questions.explanation: Plutarch wrote centuries later and drew on earlier writers such as Aristotle, but in his day Sparta staged revived 'Lycurgan' customs for visitors. He was from Chaeronea in Boeotia and wrote at length on the boys' training.

questions.stem: Thousands of small lead figurines and other offerings were excavated at the sanctuary of Artemis Orthia. Why is this evidence valuable?
options: It records the laws of Lycurgus in short inscriptions written on each of the figurines
It proves that Spartan women were barred from worshipping Artemis
It lists the names of every boy who completed the agoge at the shrine
It comes from Sparta itself and shows changing religious practice over centuries
questions.explanation: Excavated by the British School at Athens early in the twentieth century, the dedications are direct Spartan material evidence, offering a check on outsiders' writings. The figurines carry no law codes or lists of names.

questions.stem: Historians debate how far fear of the helots shaped Spartan society. Which statement best represents the debate?
options: The debate is settled, since helot records survive in Spartan archives
Some see helot revolt as Sparta's central fear; others think sources overstate it
All historians agree that the helots never once revolted against Sparta
Most historians now argue the helots were free tenant farmers who paid only a small tax
questions.explanation: Scholars such as Paul Cartledge stress helot resistance and Spartan fear, citing the Messenian revolt after the earthquake of about 464 BCE; others argue the hostile sources exaggerate it. There were real revolts, and no helot records survive.

questions.stem: According to Plutarch, the Great Rhetra was:
options: an oracle from Delphi setting out Sparta's basic political arrangements
a written law code carved on bronze tablets and set up in the agora of Sparta
a treaty between Sparta and Athens dividing the leadership of Greece
the oath sworn each month by the kings and the ephors
questions.explanation: Plutarch presents the Great Rhetra as a response from Delphi brought by Lycurgus, establishing tribes and obai, a gerousia of thirty including the kings, and regular assemblies. Spartan laws were traditionally unwritten.

questions.stem: The Great Rhetra as preserved by Plutarch includes a gerousia of thirty. How is this number made up?
options: thirty elders, with the kings attending but not voting
twenty-five elders and the five ephors of the year
twenty-nine elders and one king chosen in turn
twenty-eight elders together with the two kings
questions.explanation: The gerousia had twenty-eight members over sixty plus the two kings, making thirty. The ephors were separate officials and are not mentioned in the Rhetra.

questions.stem: A poem of Tyrtaeus sets out an order in which the kings, then the elders, then the people speak in turn. Why do historians find this significant for the Great Rhetra?
options: It suggests the Rhetra's arrangements existed by the seventh century BCE
It proves that Lycurgus personally wrote the Rhetra in the year 776 BCE
It shows that the Rhetra gave the people no say in decisions
It shows that the Rhetra was forged by Plutarch in the Roman period
questions.explanation: Tyrtaeus wrote in the seventh century, so a matching outline in his Eunomia is early evidence that something like the Rhetra was in force by then. It does not date Lycurgus, and the Rhetra did give the assembly a final say.

questions.stem: Sparta's two royal houses were the:
options: Bacchiads and Cypselids
Heraclids and Pelopids
Agiads and Eurypontids
Alcmaeonids and Pisistratids
questions.explanation: The Agiad and Eurypontid houses each supplied one king. The Alcmaeonids and Pisistratids were Athenian families, and the Bacchiads and Cypselids ruled Corinth.

questions.stem: Herodotus lists privileges of the Spartan kings. Which was one of them?
options: They held priesthoods of Zeus and received a double portion at public meals
They chose the ephors each year and could dismiss them at any time
They owned all the helots personally and could sell any of them abroad for silver
They were exempt from the agoge and were sent to be educated instead in Athens
questions.explanation: Herodotus says the kings held priesthoods of Zeus, led the army, received double portions at feasts and had duties such as judging some family cases. The ephors were elected, and heirs to the throne were in fact exempt from the agoge, though not sent to Athens.

questions.stem: After King Demaratus withdrew from a campaign against Athens in about 506 BCE, leaving his fellow king Cleomenes, Sparta changed its practice. What was the change, and what does it suggest?
options: Kings lost command of the army to the ephors, showing royal power had collapsed
The kings were replaced by elected generals, showing a move to democracy
Only one king would lead an army, showing rivalry between the kings had to be managed
Both kings had to campaign together, showing the ephors distrusted each king alone
questions.explanation: Herodotus says a law followed that both kings should not go out with the army together. The quarrel shows the dual kingship could produce damaging rivalry. Kings kept command, though ephors accompanied them.

questions.stem: Members of the gerousia were men over sixty, elected for life. Which function did the gerousia perform?
options: collected tribute from the perioikoi and paid it to the helots
prepared business for the assembly and judged capital cases
commanded the fleet in wartime and appointed the trierarchs each year
supervised the agoge in person and chose which boys would be citizens
questions.explanation: The gerousia had a probouleutic role, preparing proposals, and acted as a court for capital cases, including trials of kings. It was a conservative body of elders, not a naval or financial office.

questions.stem: Plutarch says members of the gerousia were chosen by the assembly in an unusual way. What was it?
options: the kings nominated their friends and the ephors approved them
candidates competed in a race and the fastest runners were chosen
judges in a closed building rated the loudness of the shouts for each candidate
lots were drawn each year from among all the Spartiates over the age of thirty
questions.explanation: Candidates passed through the assembly and judges out of sight judged which received the loudest shout. Aristotle called the method childish. Selection by lot was an Athenian practice.

questions.stem: Xenophon says that every month the kings and the ephors exchanged oaths. What did this show about their relationship?
options: the kings swore to rule by the laws, and the city to uphold their rule if they did
the ephors swore to obey the kings without question in war and in peace
the kings promised to step down for a whole year if the ephors found them guilty of a crime
the two groups agreed to share the command of the army month by month
questions.explanation: The monthly oath bound the kings to the laws, with the ephors promising on the city's behalf to keep their kingship secure while they did. It shows the ephors as guardians of the laws who could check the kings.

questions.stem: Full Spartan citizens, who trained in the agoge and belonged to a common mess, were called:
options: Spartiates, or homoioi
perioikoi, or dwellers around
neodamodeis, or new citizens
hypomeiones, or inferiors
questions.explanation: Full citizens were Spartiates, also called homoioi ('equals' or 'peers'). Neodamodeis were freed helots who served as soldiers, and hypomeiones were former citizens who had lost full status.

questions.stem: Aristotle says that a Spartiate who could not pay his contribution to the common mess lost his rights as a citizen. Such men became known as:
options: hypomeiones
perioikoi
helots
mothakes
questions.explanation: Losing the ability to pay mess dues meant losing full citizen status and becoming one of the hypomeiones, the 'inferiors'. Helots were unfree, and the perioikoi were free non-citizens who had never been Spartiates.

questions.stem: Xenophon describes the conspiracy of Cinadon in about 399 BCE. Cinadon was not a full citizen and hoped to rally helots, neodamodeis, hypomeiones and perioikoi against the Spartiates. What does this episode suggest?
options: Spartiates were by this time the majority of people living in Laconia
Many groups resented a shrinking citizen elite, which made Sparta's order fragile
The perioikoi had full citizen rights and wanted to share them with the helots
The ephors had lost all their power and could no longer act against conspirators in the city
questions.explanation: Cinadon's plan shows that a small body of Spartiates was surrounded by many groups excluded from power. The ephors uncovered the plot and acted quickly, so they had not lost their authority.

questions.stem: Aristotle wrote that by his time there were fewer than a thousand Spartiates. Which factor most helps explain this decline?
options: Thousands of Spartiates emigrated to found colonies in Italy and Sicily
The kings regularly expelled citizens who disagreed with their policies
Citizenship needed mess dues paid from land, and land fell into fewer hands
Spartiates were forbidden to marry, so new citizens came only from adoption
questions.explanation: Because full status required a mess contribution from land, men who lost land fell out of the citizen body, while land passed into fewer hands, including through inheritance and dowries. Spartiates were expected to marry, and Sparta founded few colonies.

questions.stem: The krypteia, as described by Plutarch drawing on Aristotle, was:
options: the hidden underground treasury where all Spartiates stored their iron currency
a secret service of young men sent into the countryside who killed helots
the council of elders that met in secret to choose the next king
a festival in which helots and Spartiates exchanged roles for a day
questions.explanation: Selected young men went out with daggers and basic supplies, hid by day and killed helots by night. It served as both a training exercise and a means of terror and control.

questions.stem: Thucydides reports that in 424 BCE the Spartans invited helots who had served well in war to claim their freedom, chose about two thousand, and then made them disappear. What does he present this as evidence of?
options: the helots had stopped resisting and were trusted as loyal soldiers
Athens had secretly arranged the killings to weaken the Spartan army
Spartan policy towards the helots was driven above all by fear of revolt
Sparta was preparing to abolish helotage and give all helots citizenship
questions.explanation: Thucydides uses the episode to show that Sparta's dealings with the helots were shaped by precautions against them; the helots most willing to claim freedom were the most likely to rebel. Sparta did also free helots as neodamodeis, but not out of trust.

questions.stem: Later writers such as Myron of Priene claim helots were made to wear dog-skin caps and were beaten each year to remind them of their status. How should a historian treat these claims?
options: as certainly true, because they were written by Spartans themselves
as certainly false, because helots were treated as equals in classical Sparta
as reliable eyewitness accounts from the time of the Messenian Wars
as possible but late, hostile reports needing earlier support
questions.explanation: These details come from Hellenistic and later writers with an interest in Spartan cruelty, so they may exaggerate or generalise. Helots were certainly not equals, but such specific claims need corroboration.

questions.stem: Which statement about Spartan women is best supported by ancient sources?
options: Women were kept indoors in separate women's quarters, as Athenian ideals expected
Women were forbidden to take part in any religious festivals
Girls took part in physical training, and women could own and inherit property
Women sat in the assembly and voted on war and peace with the men
questions.explanation: Xenophon and Plutarch say Spartan girls exercised, and Aristotle criticises how much land Spartan women held. They had no vote, were not secluded as Athenian ideals expected, and took part in festivals such as the Hyakinthia.

questions.stem: Cynisca, daughter of King Archidamus II, is famous because she:
options: wrote the maiden-songs performed by girls' choruses at Sparta
was the first woman recorded as a victor at the Olympic Games
commanded the Spartan army at the Battle of Leuctra in 371 BCE
served as the priestess of Artemis Orthia for over fifty years
questions.explanation: Cynisca won the four-horse chariot race at Olympia in the early fourth century BCE, as owner of the team. Victory went to the owner, not the driver, so wealthy Spartan women could compete in this way. Alcman wrote the maiden-songs.

questions.stem: Plutarch says that Spartan boys entered the agoge at about the age of:
options: twenty
seven
twelve
sixteen
questions.explanation: Boys left their families at seven and were organised into groups under the supervision of the paidonomos, with older youths called eirens in charge. At about twenty men could join a mess, the syssition.

questions.stem: Spartan boys were given little food and encouraged to steal more, but punished if caught. According to Xenophon, the purpose was to:
options: reduce the cost of the agoge so the city could pay the helots
prepare them for careers as merchants in the perioikic towns
make them resourceful and cunning, skills useful to a soldier
teach them that property belonged to the state and not to families
questions.explanation: Xenophon says the boys were punished not for stealing but for stealing badly, since the aim was resourcefulness. Spartiates were barred from trade, so commerce was never the goal.

questions.stem: Thucydides describes the Spartans advancing at Mantinea in 418 BCE slowly, to the music of many pipers. He says the purpose was to:
options: keep the line steady and in step, so the formation would not break apart
frighten the enemy with a war music that they believed was sacred to the god Ares
signal to the helots in camp that the battle had begun
honour Apollo Karneios, since the battle fell during his festival
questions.explanation: Thucydides explains that the pipers were not for religious reasons but to keep the men marching evenly and avoid breaking the phalanx, a common fault of large armies. Cohesion was the source of Spartan strength.

questions.stem: At Leuctra in 371 BCE, the Spartan army was defeated by the army of:
options: Thebes, led by Epaminondas
Athens, led by Iphicrates
Argos, led by its democrats
Persia, led by a satrap
questions.explanation: Epaminondas deepened his left wing to strike the Spartan right, where the king fought, and King Cleombrotus was killed. Thebes soon freed Messenia, ending Sparta's helot base there.

questions.stem: How was land worked in Spartiate households?
options: enslaved people bought abroad farmed the land under Spartiate overseers
each citizen's kleros was farmed by helots, who handed over part of the harvest
citizens farmed their own land in the morning and trained in the afternoon
perioikoi rented the land and paid their rent in silver coins to the Spartan state
questions.explanation: A Spartiate's land holding (kleros) was worked by helots tied to the land, who gave a share of the produce so their masters could meet mess contributions and train for war. Spartiates did not farm themselves.

questions.stem: Ancient writers say that instead of gold and silver coins, Spartiates used:
options: cattle as the only measure of value
bars or spits of iron as money
bronze coins stamped with an owl
shells imported from the Red Sea
questions.explanation: Xenophon and Plutarch say iron money was used to discourage the pursuit of wealth. Owl coins were Athenian silver tetradrachms.

questions.stem: Xenophon describes boys trying to steal cheeses from the altar of Artemis Orthia while others whipped them. This ritual is best understood as:
options: a punishment for helots who had failed to pay their share
a fertility rite performed by married women for Demeter
a funeral rite held each year for the kings of Sparta
a test of endurance and cunning connected with the agoge
questions.explanation: The cheese-stealing contest linked religion with the training of boys. In the Roman period it became the endurance whipping shown to tourists in a theatre built at the sanctuary, which is why later accounts can mislead.

questions.stem: The Hyakinthia, held at Amyclae, honoured Apollo and Hyacinthus. Which description of the festival is accurate?
options: it marked the death of Lycurgus, with sacrifices at his tomb
it began with a day of mourning for Hyacinthus, followed by celebration
it was a secret rite for women only, held at night in the mountains
it was held only once every four years, at the same time as the Olympic Games
questions.explanation: Ancient descriptions say the first day was solemn, without garlands or songs, then feasting, processions and choral performances followed. Herodotus says the Spartans were celebrating it in 479 BCE when Athens sought help.

questions.stem: Xenophon reports that news of the defeat at Leuctra reached Sparta during the Gymnopaedia. The ephors let the festival's choral performances continue and told the women not to lament. What does this suggest?
options: Religious duty and public composure were valued even in the face of disaster
The Gymnopaedia was unimportant, so the ephors did not bother to stop it for the news
The ephors had not yet heard any news of the defeat at Leuctra
The festival was a mourning rite, so it suited the news of Leuctra
questions.explanation: The Gymnopaedia was a major summer festival of choral dances by boys and men. Continuing it, and forbidding public grief, shows the importance of ritual and the Spartan ideal of self-control. Xenophon says the ephors were told the news.

questions.stem: Herodotus says that in 480 BCE only a small force went to Thermopylae with Leonidas, while the main army stayed at home for a time. The religious reason he gives is the:
options: Great Dionysia of Dionysus
Karneia festival of Apollo
Panathenaia of Athena
Thesmophoria of Demeter
questions.explanation: Herodotus says the Karneia, a festival of Apollo Karneios, kept the Spartans at home, and they planned to send their full force after it. The other festivals were Athenian.

questions.stem: Plutarch says Lycurgus allowed the dead to be buried inside the city near the temples. What does he say about Spartan burial practice?
options: only kings could be buried, and others were left on Mount Taygetus
every citizen was buried with his weapons and a gold death mask
burials were simple, with few grave goods and a short time of mourning
the dead were always cremated and their ashes were thrown into the Eurotas
questions.explanation: Plutarch says the dead were buried without grave goods, wrapped in a red cloak with olive leaves, and mourning lasted only a short fixed period. Kings were an exception, with elaborate public mourning.

questions.stem: Alcman, a Spartan poet of the seventh century BCE, is best known for his:
options: tragedies performed at the festival of Dionysus
history of the wars between Sparta and Messenia
maiden-songs for choruses of girls at festivals
elegies urging hoplites to stand firm in battle
questions.explanation: Alcman's partheneia were sung and danced by choruses of girls, showing a rich musical culture in early Sparta. The war elegies belong to Tyrtaeus.

questions.stem: Tyrtaeus wrote elegies during a war against the Messenians. Why are they valuable to historians?
options: they show the hoplite ideal of standing firm in the front rank for the city
they give exact figures for the number of helots in Messenia
they were written by a Messenian helot who described the Spartans' cruelty to his people
they describe the Battle of Leuctra from a Spartan point of view
questions.explanation: Tyrtaeus praised courage in the front line and shame for those who fled, and his Eunomia reflects political order. As a seventh-century source he is close to early Sparta. He wrote long before Leuctra and gives no population figures.
